stem: A custom Linux container on App Service must write temporary files that survive a container restart but not a scale-out. Where should it write?

options.text: `/home`, which is backed by persistent shared storage
`/tmp`, which is local to the container instance
The image layer, by writing into the working directory
An environment variable

explanation: On App Service, `/home` is mapped to Azure Files and is shared by every instance, so its contents survive restarts and redeploys. For custom containers this requires `WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE` to be set to true.

whyWrong.B: `/tmp` is instance-local scratch space and is lost when the container is replaced.
whyWrong.C: The image's file system is ephemeral; writes to it disappear with the container.
whyWrong.D: Environment variables hold configuration, not files.

docs.title: Configure a custom container for App Service

stem: A container-based App Service takes 90 seconds to become healthy after a restart, and requests fail during that window. Which setting stops traffic reaching an instance too early?

options.text: A health check path, so unhealthy instances are pulled from load balancing
Always On, so the app is not unloaded when it goes idle
`WEBSITES_PORT`, so requests reach the port the container listens on
ARR affinity, so a client keeps returning to the same instance

explanation: Configuring a health check path makes App Service poll each instance and exclude unhealthy ones from load balancing, which is exactly the readiness behaviour a slow-starting container needs.

whyWrong.B: Always On keeps the app from unloading when idle; it does not gate traffic during startup.
whyWrong.C: That tells the platform which port to forward to, not when the app is ready.
whyWrong.D: ARR affinity pins a client to an instance and would make the problem stickier, not better.

docs.title: Monitor App Service instances using health check

hint: The platform needs a way to know an instance is not ready yet. Which App Service setting makes it ask?

stem: You want zero-downtime deployment of a new container image to App Service, with the ability to roll back instantly. What do you use?

options.text: Deploy to a staging slot, warm it up, then swap
Update the image tag on production directly
Scale out to more instances before updating
Enable continuous deployment from the registry

explanation: A slot swap exchanges the warmed staging instances with production, so users never hit a cold instance, and swapping back restores the previous version immediately.

whyWrong.B: An in-place update restarts instances and has no rollback other than redeploying the old image.
whyWrong.C: More instances does not prevent them all restarting on a new image.
whyWrong.D: Continuous deployment automates the trigger but still updates in place unless it targets a slot.

stem: Which App Service setting makes the platform pull the container image using the app's managed identity rather than a stored registry password?

options.text: `acrUseManagedIdentityCreds`, with the identity granted `AcrPull`
`DOCKER_REGISTRY_SERVER_PASSWORD` set to the identity's client id
`WEBSITES_ENABLE_APP_SERVICE_STORAGE`
`DOCKER_ENABLE_CI`

explanation: Enabling managed identity credentials for the registry lets App Service authenticate the pull with the app's identity, which needs the `AcrPull` role. No registry username or password is stored.

whyWrong.B: That setting expects an actual password; a client id is not a credential.
whyWrong.C: That controls persistent storage mounting.
whyWrong.D: That enables the continuous-deployment webhook.

docs.title: Configure a custom container for App Service

stem: A multi-container App Service app must run an inference container alongside a sidecar that ships logs. How is this defined?

options.text: A Docker Compose file listing both containers, deployed to the app
Two separate App Service apps in the same plan
A Kubernetes manifest uploaded to App Service
Two images in the same `WEBSITES_PORT` setting

explanation: App Service supports multi-container apps defined with a Docker Compose file, where one container is the ingress target and the others run alongside it, sharing the app's network namespace.

whyWrong.B: Separate apps do not share a network namespace or a lifecycle, which is what a sidecar needs.
whyWrong.C: App Service does not accept Kubernetes manifests.
whyWrong.D: `WEBSITES_PORT` holds a port number and cannot describe a second container.

hint: Two containers, one app. App Service takes a familiar multi-container format to describe that.

stem: You need to remove old image versions from a registry automatically while keeping the most recent ones. What supports this?

options.text: A retention policy that removes untagged manifests after a set number of days
Content trust, which signs images so consumers can verify the publisher
Geo-replication, which copies images to replicas in other regions
A private endpoint, which limits registry access to a virtual network

explanation: ACR expires untagged manifests on a retention policy. Pushing a new build to the same tag leaves the previous manifest untagged, so the policy reclaims it after the configured number of days.

whyWrong.B: Content trust signs images so consumers can verify publisher and integrity.
whyWrong.C: Geo-replication copies content to more regions, increasing storage rather than reducing it.
whyWrong.D: Private endpoints control network access.

stem: A multi-step ACR task must build an image, run its tests, and push only if the tests pass. Which mechanism supports this?

options.text: A multi-step task defined in a YAML file with `build`, `cmd` and `push` steps
Three separate quick tasks chained by a pipeline
A base image update trigger
An ACR webhook per step

explanation: Multi-step tasks describe a sequence in YAML, with the push step depending on the earlier steps succeeding. A failing test command stops the task before anything is published.

whyWrong.B: That works but moves the orchestration outside ACR, which the multi-step format exists to avoid.
whyWrong.C: Base image triggers decide when a task runs, not what steps it performs.
whyWrong.D: Webhooks notify external systems after events; they do not sequence a build.

hint: This is more than one operation with a condition between them, so it cannot be a single quick build. ACR describes those in a file.

stem: Which authentication method allows a container instance to pull from ACR with no credential stored anywhere, and is scoped to that workload?

options.text: A user-assigned managed identity granted `AcrPull`
The registry admin account
A service principal secret in an environment variable
Anonymous pull access

explanation: A managed identity has no secret to store or rotate, and granting it `AcrPull` limits it to reading images. A user-assigned identity can additionally be reused across resources and survives their recreation.

whyWrong.B: The admin account is a shared credential with full access and is disabled by default.
whyWrong.C: That stores a secret, which the requirement excludes.
whyWrong.D: Anonymous pull removes authentication entirely and exposes the images publicly.

stem: An image tagged `latest` is deployed but instances are running an older build. What practice avoids this class of problem?

options.text: Deploy immutable, uniquely versioned tags such as a build number or digest
Set the image pull policy to never
Enable geo-replication so all regions have the same image
Push `latest` twice to force a refresh

explanation: A mutable tag makes what is running ambiguous — a cached layer or a not-yet-restarted instance can serve an old build. Unique tags, or pinning to a digest, make the deployed version explicit and reproducible.

whyWrong.B: That guarantees the stale local image is used forever.
whyWrong.C: Replication distributes whatever the tag points at, including the ambiguity.
whyWrong.D: Pushing again does not invalidate what is already running.

stem: A Container App must call an Azure OpenAI endpoint that only accepts traffic from a specific virtual network. What must be true of the environment?

options.text: It must be created with VNet integration into a subnet that can reach the endpoint
The app must use external ingress
The app must run at least two replicas
The environment must be in the same resource group as the endpoint

explanation: Networking is a property of the Container Apps environment, and the VNet is chosen when the environment is created — it cannot be added later. Egress then originates from that subnet and can reach private endpoints.

whyWrong.B: Ingress governs inbound traffic; this is an outbound requirement.
whyWrong.C: Replica count has no bearing on network reachability.
whyWrong.D: Resource group is an organisational boundary, not a network one.

stem: A Container App scales between 0 and 30 replicas on queue length, but during a burst the downstream database is overwhelmed. What is the appropriate control?

options.text: Lower `maxReplicas` so concurrency against the database is bounded
Raise `minReplicas` so replicas are always warm
Remove the scale rule so the app never scales
Switch to a cron scale rule

explanation: The maximum replica count is the back-pressure valve. Capping it bounds how much concurrency reaches the database while still letting the queue absorb the burst — work is delayed rather than dropped.

whyWrong.B: Warm replicas address cold start, not peak concurrency.
whyWrong.C: Never scaling turns a burst into a permanent backlog.
whyWrong.D: A schedule does not correspond to when the burst arrives.

docs.title: Set scaling rules in Container Apps

hint: The queue is not the constraint - the database is. Ask which knob bounds how much concurrency ever reaches it.

stem: Which Container Apps job trigger type suits work that must run once per message on a Service Bus queue?

options.text: An event trigger with a KEDA scaler on the queue
A schedule trigger running every minute
A manual trigger invoked by the producer
A schedule trigger with a cron expression of every second

explanation: Event-driven jobs start an execution in response to a KEDA scaler, so each unit of queued work gets its own run that exits when finished — no idle replica between messages.

whyWrong.B: Polling adds up to a minute of latency and starts runs when there is nothing to do.
whyWrong.C: That couples the producer to the job's lifecycle and loses the queue's durability.
whyWrong.D: A one-second schedule is wasteful and still not event-driven.

stem: You deploy a new revision and want 5% of traffic on it for an hour before committing. Which pair of settings is required?

options.text: Multiple revision mode, with traffic weights of 95 and 5 across the two revisions
Single revision mode, with a 5% scale rule on the new revision
Multiple revision mode, with the new revision deactivated
Two container apps behind a load balancer

explanation: Weighted traffic between revisions requires multiple revision mode; in single revision mode all traffic goes to the latest and any weights are ignored. Both revisions must also be active to receive traffic.

whyWrong.B: Scale rules control replica count, not the share of requests a revision receives.
whyWrong.C: A deactivated revision receives no traffic at all.
whyWrong.D: That reimplements a built-in feature with more moving parts.

hint: Splitting traffic requires more than one revision to be addressable at once. Check what mode that needs, and that weights must total 100.

stem: Where do you look to find out why a Container Apps revision shows as failed with no application output?

options.text: System logs, which record image pull failures and probe results
Console logs, which record the application's stdout
Application Insights request telemetry
The subscription activity log

explanation: No application output is itself the clue: the container never got far enough to print anything. System logs are the platform's account of provisioning the revision, including registry authentication failures and failed probes.

whyWrong.B: Console logs carry stdout and stderr, which is exactly what is missing.
whyWrong.C: Application Insights only receives data once the instrumented app runs.
whyWrong.D: The activity log records the deployment request, not the container's fate.

stem: A deployment manifest sets a memory request of 2Gi and a limit of 2Gi. What does this guarantee?

options.text: The pod is scheduled only where 2Gi is available and is killed if it exceeds 2Gi
The pod can burst above 2Gi when the node has spare memory
The pod is never evicted under node memory pressure
Kubernetes reserves 2Gi of swap for the pod

explanation: The request drives scheduling and the limit is enforced at runtime. Setting them equal gives the pod the Guaranteed quality-of-service class, which makes it the last to be evicted — but exceeding the limit still means an OOM kill.

whyWrong.B: Bursting is possible only when the limit exceeds the request.
whyWrong.C: Guaranteed pods are evicted last, not never.
whyWrong.D: Kubernetes disables swap by default and does not reserve it.

stem: An inference pod loads a 4 GB model and takes two minutes to start. A liveness probe with a 30-second threshold is configured. What happens, and what fixes it?

options.text: The pod is killed and restarts forever; add a startup probe so liveness only begins after startup completes
The pod starts normally; liveness probes do not apply during startup
The pod is marked unready but keeps running; add a readiness probe
The pod is evicted for exceeding its memory limit; raise the limit

explanation: A liveness probe that fails during a slow start produces an endless restart loop — the container never gets the two minutes it needs. A startup probe suspends the liveness check until the app reports started, which is exactly what this pattern is for.

whyWrong.B: Liveness probes do apply from the container's start unless a startup probe defers them.
whyWrong.C: Readiness controls traffic; it does not stop liveness restarting the container.
whyWrong.D: The symptom described is a probe timeout, not an OOM kill.

docs.title: Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes

hint: Liveness is asking whether it is alive, but the container is still starting. Ask which probe exists precisely to cover slow starts.

stem: Which manifest object holds non-secret configuration that several pods read as environment variables?

options.text: A ConfigMap
A Secret
A PersistentVolumeClaim
A ServiceAccount

explanation: ConfigMaps hold non-confidential key-value configuration, consumed as environment variables via `configMapKeyRef` or mounted as files. Secrets are the equivalent for confidential values.

whyWrong.B: Secrets are for confidential data; using them for plain settings adds no benefit and obscures intent.
whyWrong.C: A claim requests storage.
whyWrong.D: A service account provides an identity for the pod.

docs.title: Configure a pod to use a ConfigMap

stem: Pods are Pending and cluster autoscaler logs show it will not add nodes. The pods request a GPU the node pool does not offer. What is the fix?

options.text: Add a node pool with the required GPU SKU and matching labels or taints
Increase the autoscaler's maximum node count on the existing pool
Remove the resource requests from the pods
Restart the autoscaler

explanation: The autoscaler only adds nodes of the types already defined in a node pool. If no pool can ever satisfy the request, adding more of the same nodes cannot help — you need a pool with the right hardware.

whyWrong.B: More nodes of a SKU without GPUs still cannot host the pods.
whyWrong.C: Dropping the request would schedule the pod onto hardware that cannot run it.
whyWrong.D: The autoscaler is behaving correctly; there is nothing to restart.

hint: The autoscaler only adds nodes it believes would let the pod schedule. If no pool can ever satisfy the request, it will not try.

stem: Which AKS add-on lets a Deployment scale on the length of a Service Bus queue?

options.text: KEDA
The cluster autoscaler
The vertical pod autoscaler
Container insights

explanation: KEDA supplies external metrics to the horizontal autoscaler, so a Deployment can scale on queue depth — and down to zero — rather than on CPU.

whyWrong.B: The cluster autoscaler adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled; it does not decide replica counts.
whyWrong.C: VPA adjusts a pod's resource requests rather than the number of pods.
whyWrong.D: Container insights collects telemetry and does not scale anything.

stem: Match each pod symptom to its usual cause.

choices.text: Registry authentication or a wrong tag
The container exits shortly after starting
No node can satisfy the resource request
Registry authentication or a wrong tag
The container exits shortly after starting
No node can satisfy the resource request
Registry authentication or a wrong tag
The container exits shortly after starting
No node can satisfy the resource request

explanation: These three cover most pod failures and they are distinguished by how far the pod got. Pending means the scheduler never placed it. `ImagePullBackOff` means it was placed but the image could not be fetched. `CrashLoopBackOff` means the image ran and the process exited — the only one where application logs will tell you anything.
hint: Decode each by when it fails: before the image is available, after the container starts, or before the scheduler places it at all.

stem: A pod using workload identity fails to acquire a token. Which element is most commonly missing?

options.text: The federated credential linking the Kubernetes service account to the managed identity
A Kubernetes Secret holding the identity's client secret
A LoadBalancer service for the pod
A PersistentVolumeClaim for the token cache

explanation: Workload identity works by federating the service account's projected token with Entra ID. The federated credential — naming the cluster's OIDC issuer, the namespace and the service account — is what establishes that trust, and its absence is the usual cause of token failures.

whyWrong.B: The entire point is that no secret exists.
whyWrong.C: Services expose pods to traffic and are unrelated to identity.
whyWrong.D: Tokens are projected into the pod automatically; no volume claim is needed.

docs.title: Microsoft Entra Workload ID with AKS

hint: Workload identity is a trust relationship between two identities. Ask which object declares that the Kubernetes side is allowed to act as the Azure one.

stem: Which command shows recent cluster events ordered so the newest appear last, useful for diagnosing a failing rollout?

options.text: `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp`
`kubectl logs --all-containers`
`kubectl top pod`
`kubectl describe node`

explanation: Events are returned unsorted by default, which makes them hard to read during an incident. Sorting by last timestamp gives a chronological view of scheduling decisions, image pulls, probe failures and evictions.

whyWrong.B: Logs show application output, not cluster decisions.
whyWrong.C: top reports resource usage.
whyWrong.D: describe node covers one node's capacity and conditions rather than cluster-wide events.

stem: Put the phases of a Kubernetes rolling update in order for a Deployment with `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`.

options.text: A new pod is created with the updated image
The new pod passes its readiness probe and joins the Service endpoints
An old pod is removed from the endpoints and sent SIGTERM
The old pod terminates and the cycle repeats for the next replica

explanation: With `maxUnavailable: 0` capacity may never drop, so a replacement must be ready before an old pod is taken away — surge first, then retire. That ordering is what makes the update zero-downtime, provided readiness genuinely reflects the app's ability to serve.
